newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: BHP sees "much higher" performance by 2000.
newsitem.headline: BHP sees "much higher" performance by 2000.

text.p: Australia's largest listed company The Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd (BHP) assured investors of much higher performance by the year 2000, but again played down hopes of an immediate improvement.
BHP managing director John Prescott said in a television interview broadcast on Sunday that he took considerable blame for the steel, mining and petroleum group's recent woes.

On Friday, BHP reported a plunge in annual net profit for the year to May 31, 1997, to A$410 million (US$305 million), its worst in a decade, after sustaining one-off net abnormal losses totalling A$976 million.
The abnormal losses were mainly made up of write-downs to BHP's global asset base.

The value of its new North American copper operations was slashed by A$550 million. The value of steel assets was cut by A$220 million, minerals assets by A$189 million and petroleum assets by A$124 million.
Before abnormals, BHP's earnings of almost A$1.39 billion for the year ended May 31 were in line with market forecasts.

Share analysts immediately began revising up their earnings forecasts for 1997/98, based on a lower depreciation charge on the trimmed-down asset base as well as signs of an upturn in the copper and steel businesses.
Before the profit result, BHP was expected to report a pre-abnormal net profit of around A$1.8 billion for 1997/98. Analysts are now revising it closer to A$2 billion.
"I want to see a significant improvement over the next two or three years," Prescott told the Channel Nine network's Business Sunday programme.
"I have indicated to the market that I think this next year (1997/98) will be fairly flat, but we have a number of restructuring initiatives underway, notably in steel but also elsewhere."
"I would hope that within three years we would have achieved a much higher level of performance," he said in the interview, which was taped on Friday.
Prescott said he took considerable responsibility for BHP's recent problem with underperforming assets, but would not be drawn on whether senior executives would take another pay cut.
"We have not assessed bonuses for this year at this stage," he said.
BHP's array of new projects are being reviewed in the context of the group's new performance benchmark, which is to be among the best 20 percent of companies in its class.
"We are reassessing all our projects to see they meet our expectations, but basically I expect most of them will go forward. There may be some adjustments here and there," Prescott said.
Despite the capital demands of developing new projects, BHP aims to keep its gearing levels relatively low, in line with a trend among resource companies to lessen their reliance on debt, he added.
